headline: Wall Street closes at fresh records on Hormuz de-escalation hopes while KSE-100 slips 0.63% on institutional profit-taking and oil tumbles over 5%
mood: Cautiously constructive · oil and the Fed are the swing factors

snapshot.label: US 10Y / 2Y
snapshot.delta: Warsh hold · Sept hike odds rising

five_things.html: The S&P 500 (+1.79% to 7,736.52), Dow (+1.71% to 54,085.88, above 54,000 for the first time) and Nasdaq (+2.59% to 26,584.99) all closed at records on Tuesday as easing US-Iran tensions over the Strait of Hormuz and a tech rebound drove the strongest rally in months (CNN, CNBC).

The KSE-100 fell 0.63% to 177,083.22 (−1,116.80 pts), giving back part of Monday's rally as institutional selling hit banks, E&P and cement names — breadth turned negative at 161 advancers vs 295 decliners on 711.3m shares (Rs25.9bn) (Express Tribune, Trading Economics).

Brent (−5.9% to $78.87) and WTI (down over 5%, trading $76.60–$82.32) tumbled as diplomacy hopes eased Strait of Hormuz supply risk, even as seven OPEC+ producers layered on 188,000 bpd of extra August supply (Trading Economics, Saudi Gazette).

Gold held near $4,076 and silver near $58.74 as Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish-tinted 29 July hold (FOMC voted 9-3 to stand pat) left markets pricing rising odds of a September hike rather than a cut (CNBC, Trading Economics).

CPI eased to 9.2% YoY in July from 11.1% in June, giving the SBP room to hold its policy rate at 11.5% for a second straight meeting, while Gulf non-oil PMIs (Saudi 53.1) stayed comfortably expansionary even as the UAE's cooled toward a multi-year low (Business Recorder, Semafor).

matrix.local_html: Tuesday's session saw the KSE-100 retreat 0.63% to 177,083.22, shedding 1,116.80 points as institutional profit-taking hit heavyweight sectors — commercial banks, oil & gas exploration, cement and fertilizer — at elevated resistance levels. Breadth turned negative, with 295 decliners against 161 advancers (39 unchanged) on 711.3 million shares (Rs25.9bn); foreign investors were still net buyers to the tune of Rs166.3m. Meezan Bank, PSO, Kapco, Power Cement and Millat Tractors added a combined 175 points, but UBL, Engro Holdings, OGDC, Lucky Cement and PPL erased roughly 580 points on selective profit-taking. On the macro front, headline CPI eased to 9.2% YoY in July from 11.1% in June, giving the SBP room to hold its policy rate at 11.5% for a second straight meeting on 27 July. Six-month KIBOR is tracking near 11.70–11.90% (EST.), broadly in line with the policy rate. The IMF's Executive Board cleared the third EFF/second RSF review on 8 May, unlocking roughly $1.1bn (EFF) and $220m (RSF); the next review is expected in H2 2026.
matrix.gcc_html: Gulf oil producers added to August supply as seven OPEC+ members agreed to raise output by 188,000 bpd — Saudi Arabia and Russia each contributing 62,000 bpd, with smaller increases from Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman — the fifth consecutive monthly increase as the group unwinds 2023's voluntary cuts. That extra supply landed just as Brent slid nearly 6% to $78.87, a three-week-plus low, on hopes for a reopened Strait of Hormuz — a double-barrelled bearish setup for crude that nonetheless keeps the Gulf's non-oil diversification story intact. Saudi Arabia's non-oil PMI held at a still-robust 53.1 in July (53.3 in June) on firmer domestic demand, even as export orders fell for a fifth straight month on high freight costs. The UAE's non-oil private sector cooled toward its softest pace in several years (EST. low-51 handle) as regional disruptions weighed on new orders — a mixed but still-expansionary signal for Vision 2030-linked non-oil diversification and PIF-backed giga-projects.
matrix.global_html: Wall Street closed at fresh records on Tuesday — the S&P 500 jumped 1.79% to 7,736.52, the Dow added 907.47 points (+1.71%) to close above 54,000 for the first time, and the Nasdaq surged 2.59% to 26,584.99, powered by a tech rebound, strong earnings and easing US-Iran tensions over Hormuz. Bonds told a more cautious story: the 10-year yield sits near 4.63% and the 2-year at 4.21%, with markets pricing rising odds the Fed hikes rather than cuts in September after Chair Kevin Warsh's FOMC voted 9-3 to hold on 29 July, a decision that has left his inflation-fighting credibility under scrutiny. Separately, Washington's trade agenda intensified: a 50% ad valorem tariff on Canadian goods takes effect 19 August, alongside Section 301 forced-labor duties of 10–12.5% on roughly 60 economies that took effect 24 July.

legislative.policy_html: Finance Act 2026 imposed a 5% withholding tax (10% for non-filers) on digital content creators' social media earnings, effective 1 July; banks began deducting it at source from 30 July.
legislative.impact_html: Wins: FBR digitisation vendors, compliant formal-sector filers. Loses: social-media creators/influencers (especially non-filers facing a 10% deduction), platforms monetising Pakistani audiences.

legislative.policy_html: Saudi Arabia's new Companies Law mandates beneficial-ownership disclosure and a unified commercial register; the UAE's Cabinet Decision No. 59 of 2026 competition-law regulations took effect 30 July.
legislative.impact_html: Wins: institutional investors and dealmakers gaining transparency, multinationals already compliant. Loses: opaque shell structures, SMEs absorbing new compliance overhead.

legislative.policy_html: Washington's 50% tariff on Canadian goods (cement, furniture, textiles) takes effect 19 August; Section 301 forced-labor tariffs of 10–12.5% on roughly 60 economies are already live since 24 July.
legislative.impact_html: Wins: US domestic manufacturers in tariffed categories. Loses: Canadian exporters, US importers/retailers and consumers facing higher input costs.

desk_stance_html: Desk view: Tuesday's pullback reads as institutional profit-taking after a sharp advance, not a trend reversal — breadth stayed negative (161 advancers vs 295 decliners) but foreign flows remained net positive (Rs166.3m) and large-cap banks/energy names absorbed most of the selling. Global tailwinds hold: a sharp Brent/WTI drawdown on Hormuz de-escalation hopes is disinflationary for Pakistan's import bill, and Wall Street's record run keeps risk appetite supportive for EM flows. Watch 176,000 as the first floor; a close below opens 174,500. On the upside, reclaiming 178,200 re-opens Monday's high near 179,500. All levels are indicative desk estimates, not recommendations.

linkedin_text:
🌅 Economic Vibes — Morning Brief | Wednesday, 05 August 2026

Wall Street closed at records overnight while the KSE-100 took a breather — here's what the desk is watching this morning.

THE OVERNIGHT TAPE
S&P 500 +1.79% to 7,736.52, Dow +1.71% to 54,085.88 (first close above 54,000), Nasdaq +2.59% to 26,584.99 — all-time highs driven by easing US-Iran tensions over the Strait of Hormuz and a tech rebound. US 10Y sits at 4.63%, 2Y at 4.21%, with markets pricing rising odds of a Fed hike (not a cut) in September after Chair Kevin Warsh's FOMC voted 9-3 to hold on 29 July.

PAKISTAN
KSE-100 slipped 0.63% to 177,083.22 (−1,116.80 pts) on institutional profit-taking in banks, E&P and cement, as breadth turned negative (161 advancers vs 295 decliners, 711.3m shares, Rs25.9bn) — though foreign investors stayed net buyers (Rs166.3m). UBL, Engro Holdings, OGDC, Lucky Cement and PPL led the drag; Meezan Bank, PSO and Power Cement held up. On the macro side: CPI eased to 9.2% YoY in July from 11.1%, and the SBP held its policy rate at 11.5% for a second straight meeting. The IMF's Executive Board cleared the third EFF/second RSF review in May, unlocking roughly $1.3bn combined; the next review is expected in H2 2026.

GCC
Seven OPEC+ producers added 188,000 bpd of August supply even as Brent (−5.9% to $78.87) and WTI (down 5%+) tumbled on Hormuz de-escalation hopes. Saudi's non-oil PMI held at 53.1 in July; the UAE's cooled toward its softest pace in years on regional disruptions — a mixed but still-expansionary read for Vision 2030 diversification.

GLOBAL
Gold is holding near $4,076, silver near $58.74, as Fed policy uncertainty keeps havens bid even with equities at records. Washington's trade agenda is heating up: a 50% tariff on Canadian goods lands 19 August, and Section 301 forced-labor tariffs (10–12.5% on ~60 economies) are already in force since 24 July.

LEGISLATIVE TRACKER
Pakistan's Finance Act 2026 brings a 5% withholding tax (10% for non-filers) on social media earnings, now being deducted at source by banks — a cost for creators, a win for compliance-tech vendors.
Saudi's new Companies Law and the UAE's Cabinet Decision 59/2026 competition rules tighten disclosure — wins for institutional investors, added overhead for SMEs.
US tariffs on Canada (50%) and forced-labor goods (10–12.5%, ~60 economies) raise input costs for importers and retailers even as they shield targeted US manufacturers.

THE DAY AHEAD
KSE-100: support 176,000 (deeper at 174,500), pivot 177,083 (Tuesday's close), resistance 178,200 (Monday's close/high, then 179,500).
Desk view: Tuesday's dip reads as profit-taking, not reversal — falling oil is a tailwind for Pakistan's import bill, and global risk appetite stays supportive. All levels are indicative desk estimates, not recommendations.
